subject: History
framework: National Curriculum in England (2014): History programmes of study, Key Stages 1 to 3, with EYFS Understanding the World
statusNote: Key Stage 1 to 3 statutory content and period lists were re-read from the gov.uk National Curriculum history programme of study (page read through a fetch tool that returns summaries, checked against the earlier reading). EYFS Understanding the World: Past and Present was read in the 13 July 2026 statutory framework (in force 1 September 2026) and the Reception row matches it. Year allocation is a recommended sequence, not statutory; the National Curriculum sets content by key stage. Year units follow the school's existing unit titles. History is taught from Year 1 to Year 9 only; it is not offered at Key Stage 4. Year 1 was rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA Year 1 Curriculum Pack: one unit per half term, following Tarbiyyah Primary's Cornerstones projects (2026-27 order), White Rose maths and Little Wandle phonics. Years 2 to 9 were rebuilt in November 2026 to the TGA curriculum packs (docs/curriculum-packs/y2.md to y9.md): one unit per half term, titled by half term so the portal planner places each one. November 2026 alignment: Years 1 to 6 keep the Tarbiyyah Primary Long Term Plan 2026-27 project order, with each project's history content taken from the school's 2023-24 curriculum maps and history long-term plan (for example Year 3 Mighty Metals teaches the History of Sports Tournaments, as in the map). November 2026 alignment with the school's own files: Years 7 to 9 follow the Tarbiyyah Secondary History Curriculum Intent (its KS3 programme overview sets the order and topics) and Hodder's Understanding History: Key Stage 3 scheme of work (2019; a publisher's generic scheme, in the school folder as 'Progress in History Scheme of Work KS3'), whose lesson numbers are named on each unit. The founding year teaches Spring 1 to Summer 2 from Mon 11 Jan 2027. History is not taught at KS4; the school's KS4 History scheme (Weimar and Nazi Germany) is not used.

purpose: Build coherent knowledge of Britain and the wider world and spark curiosity about the past.
Use evidence, interpretations and second-order concepts such as change, cause, similarity and significance.
Link local, national and international history across short and long timescales.

statements: Talk about the lives and roles of people around them.
Compare past and present using their own experiences and class books.
Understand the past through books read in class and storytelling.
Use time words and place events and objects in order on a timeline.
Compare ways of life in different periods.
Use stories, pictures and sources to ask and answer questions.
Changes within living memory.
Events beyond living memory that are nationally or globally significant, such as the Great Fire of London.
Lives of significant individuals, compared across periods.
Significant historical events, people and places in the local area.
Build secure chronological knowledge and narratives, connecting local, British and world history.
Note connections, contrasts and trends over time with historical terms.
Ask questions on change, cause, similarity and significance; understand how sources build knowledge.
Britain from the Stone Age to the Iron Age.
The Roman Empire and its impact on Britain.
Anglo-Saxon and Scots settlement of Britain.
The Viking and Anglo-Saxon struggle for the kingdom of England up to Edward the Confessor.
A local history study.
An aspect or theme in British history beyond 1066.
An overview of the earliest civilisations, with a depth study of one.
Ancient Greece: life, achievements and influence on the western world.
A non-European society contrasting with British history: early Islamic civilisation, Maya or Benin.
Deepen chronological understanding and trace trends over long periods.
Use second-order concepts with more sophistication.
Pursue self-framed enquiries; evaluate sources and understand why interpretations differ.
Church, state and society in medieval Britain, 1066-1509.
Church, state and society in Britain, 1509-1745.
Ideas, political power, industry and empire: Britain, 1745-1901.
Challenges for Britain, Europe and the wider world, 1901 to the present, including the Holocaust.
A local history study and a theme in British history from before 1066.
At least one study of a significant society or issue in world history, such as Mughal India, Qing China or 20th-century USA.

toKS4: History is not offered at Key Stage 4: the subject ends in Year 9. The KS3 skills carry into other KS4 subjects: chronology, cause and consequence and source analysis into Islamic Studies (4IS1 Section A, the life of the Prophet and the early Muslim community); context and interpretation into English Literature (4ET1 AO4, for example Jacobean England for Macbeth and 1930s America for Of Mice and Men); and change over time into Geography (development and urban change). Pupils who want GCSE History later can build on the Year 7 to Year 9 units.

links.topic: Industrial Revolution, urban growth and 1854 Soho cholera outbreak
links.how: History gives causes and public health context; Geography gives mapping and urbanisation

links.topic: Roman Britain: roads, towns, rivers and settlement
links.how: History tells the story; Geography explains routes, relief and settlement sites
Science explains materials, engines and infection; History shows their effect on society

links.topic: Scholars of the golden age: astronomy, medicine and optics
links.how: Science explains the ideas; History places them in Baghdad's House of Wisdom
Maths provides number lines and data skills; History applies them to dates and population data
English teaches structure and inference; History uses them in accounts and source work

links.topic: Christianity and Islam in history, including Muslim soldiers in the First World War
links.how: RE explains beliefs; History explains their role in events and societies
Geography covers resource distribution and trade; History explains industry and empire
Art analyses form and message; History uses it as source evidence
Citizenship explains modern law and rights; History traces limits on royal power

gaps: Note: the year-by-year split is a recommended sequence, not statutory.
